abstract: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) frequently affects extremely preterm and low birth weight infants, with current treatments lacking specificity. Enhancing extra-uterine preterm alveoli development and repairing damage are crucial for BPD management. Here we show that exosomes derived from human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hucMSCs-Exos) can enhance fetal lung development in mice by delivering specific contents. Briefly, hucMSCs-Exos were extracted using ultracentrifugation and identified by transmission electron microscopy (TEM), flow cytometry, Western blot (WB), and nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA). These exosomes were then administered to pregnant mice via tail vein injection. Embryonic lung tissues were collected at E13.5 and E18.5 via cesarean section and analyzed using hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining, immunofluorescence, and TEM. Proteomic analysis was conducted to identify protein components in the exosomes, and WB was used to assess protein expression changes. hucMSCs-Exos from full-term infants were more effective in promoting cell proliferation than those from preterm infants. In vivo, full-term hucMSCs-Exos significantly enhanced alveolarization in fetal lung tissues. Proteomic analysis revealed higher Wnt5a expression in full-term hucMSCs-Exos, and further experiments confirmed a direct interaction between Wnt5a and ROCK1. WB also showed increased expression of the autophagy marker LC3B in the lung tissues of mice treated with full-term exosomes. In conclusion, term hucMSCs-Exos may directly regulate the phosphorylation of ROCK1 in mouse lung tissue through naturally enriched Wnt5a, thus promoting autophagy of AT2 cells and lamellar body development, and ultimately enhance the alveolarization and reducing the incidence of BPD in premature infants. Graphical Abstract Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s12015-024-10824-1.
methods:
Materials and Methods
Study and Approval
Human umbilical cord was acquired from term and preterm infants on birth (all individuals and their parents provided informed consent to participate in this study and approval was provided by Medical Research Ethics Committee of West China Second University Hospital, Sichuan University, Medical Research 2022 Ethics Approval No. 290). All animal experiments have been approved by the China Ethics Committee and West China Second University Hospital Institutional Animal Care, and performed in accordance with the ethical standards, and raised in Animal Care.
Primary Cell Culture
The hucMSCs were isolated and cultured following a modified explant method, as described in our last study. In summary, the umbilical cord was cleaned with Dulbecco’s phosphate-buffered saline (DPBS, Invitrogen, USA), then longitudinally cut, and the arteries and veins were all removed. Following that, the soft gel tissues were dissected into small pieces (1 ~ 3 mm [
3
]) and placed individually on 6-well plate with Modified Eagle Medium-α (MEM-α, Gibco, USA), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Invitrogen, USA) and penicillin/streptomycin. The plates were then incubated for 10 ~ 12 days at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO
2
. During the incubation period, supplemented MEM-α was periodically added, until the umbilical cord tissue was eventually removed. After washing the plates three times with MEM-α, the plastic adherent cell colonies were trypsinized (TrypLE™ Express (1X), Gibco, USA) and maintained in culture using MEM-α supplemented with 10% FBS and penicillin/streptomycin. At passage 3 ~ 5, hucMSCs were expanded in 10-stack Corning CellSTACK
®
cell culture chambers. It is important to note that multiple umbilical cords were used, with each cord giving rise to individual MSC colonies. Each independent in vivo experiment utilized a distinct Exos preparation.
Exos Harvest and Isolation
The isolation and characterization of Exos were carried out in accordance with the guidelines provided by the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles (ISEV) in their 2018 Minimal Information for Studies of Extracellular Vesicles (MISEV) publications [
47
,
48
]. Exos, denoting small EVs (sEVs) with diameters ranging approximately between 40 and 150 nm, along with the expression of well-characterized Exos markers such as TSG101, ALIX, CD9, CD63, CD81, and Flotillin-1 (FLOT-1), were procured from the conditioned media (CM) of hucMSCs cultures. These cultures were maintained for 48 h in serum-free media. The isolation process involved sequential differential centrifugation procedures to sequentially eliminate cells (750 ×g for 10 min), cellular debris (3000 ×g for 20 min), and apoptotic remnants (12,000 ×g for 45 min), all of which were conducted under strictly controlled 4℃ conditions. Subsequently, the CM underwent ultra-centrifugation using a Type50.2 Ti rotor for a duration of 1.5 h at 120,000 ×g and 4 °C. The resulting pellet was meticulously collected and then transferred to a SW41 Ti rotor for an additional centrifugation period of 2 h at the same speed and temperature. Finally, the supernatants were carefully removed, and the Exos pellet was re-suspended in 200 µL of Dulbecco’s Phosphate-Buffered Saline (DPBS, Invitrogen, USA).
Transmission Electron Microscopy
To evaluate the morphology of Exos, a 5 µL sample from the sEV preparation was adsorbed onto a carbon-coated grid (Electron Microscopy Sciences, USA) for a duration of one minute. The grids were rendered hydrophilic through a 30-seconds exposure to glow discharge. Any surplus liquid was then carefully eliminated, and the grids were subsequently cleansed with a single drop of water. Following the removal of any remaining excess liquid, the grids were stained with 1% uranyl acetate for a period of 15 s. The morphology of the adsorbed Exos was subsequently examined under a transmission electron microscopy (JEM-1400FLASH, JP).
For lung tissue observation, the following steps are used to conduct the experiment: Fixation: The samples were pre-fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde (customer’s fixation), followed by postfixation with 1% osmium tetroxide. Dehydration: The samples were dehydrated stepwise with acetone, with the dehydration agent concentration gradient of 30% → 50% → 70% → 80% → 90% → 95% → 100% (change the 100% concentration three times). Infiltration: The dehydration agent and Epon-812 embedding medium were mixed in proportions of 3:1, 1:1, and 1:3, respectively, for sequential infiltration. Embedding: The sample was embedded with pure Epon-812 embedding medium. Semi-thin localization and ultra-thin sectioning: the mouse lung tissue alveolar region was selected under a light microscope by observing semi-thin sections, and ultra-thin sections of 60 ~ 90 nm were cut using an ultra-thin sectioning machine and collected on copper grids. Staining: The sections were first stained with uranyl acetate for 10 ~ 15 min, followed by staining with lead citrate for 1 ~ 2 min at room temperature. Next, using the JEM-1400FLASH transmission electron microscope (TOK, JP) to collect images of the copper mesh, each copper mesh is first observed in low magnification to view the entire tissue, then images of the areas to be observed are collected, and specific lesions are examined.
Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis
The size and concentration distributions of Exos were meticulously assessed using NTA (ZetaView, Particle Metrix, GER) on a state-of-the-art Nanoparticle Tracking Analyses system, adhering to the method previously outlined [
49
]. During the procedure, the samples were introduced into the pump, and the Brownian motion of the nanoparticles was meticulously monitored. Concurrently, the particle size was determined based on the Stokes-Einstein equation, while the particle concentration in the solution was accurately computed from the number of tracked particles. Prior to analysis, the Exos samples were carefully diluted in vesicle-free ultrapure water to ensure optimal measurement conditions.
Exosomes Markers Characterization
We commenced the characterization of the isolated exosomes by employing conventional methodologies, initiating with WB analysis on the extracted exosomes. We utilized CD9, CD63, and TSG101 (Abiowell, CHN) as our positive markers, with Calnexin (Abiowell, CHN) serving as the negative control. To discern exosomes from protein aggregates, we resorted to nanoparticle flow cytometry for the analysis of the exosomes’ surface markers. Post-determination of concentration via NTA, the samples were adjusted to a concentration of 1 × 10
7
particles/mL using DPBS. A 100 µL aliquot of this diluted sample was then incubated at ambient temperature, shielded from light, with 5 µL each of PE-conjugated CD9, PE-conjugated CD63, and APC-conjugated CD81 antibodies (Invitrogen, USA) for a duration of 45 min. To ensure adequate mixing, the samples were subjected to intermittent shaking throughout the incubation period. For flow cytometric analysis, we utilized the Cytoflex instrument (Beckman Coulter, USA), equipped with a 405/10 filter and the Event Rate set to a high level. The detection of scatter signals was optimized using the VSSC-H parameter, with the threshold configured to Height. Prior to analysis, the instrument was meticulously cleaned with a 1% sodium hypochlorite solution, filtered through a 0.1 μm Millex-VV syringe filter unit from Merck, followed by a rinse with ultrapure water, also filtered through a Millex-VV syringe filter. Calibration of the optical path was achieved using particle beads (ApogeeMix, ESP). Upon the detection of positive signals, data were meticulously collected and recorded. Subsequently, we introduced 0.1% Triton X-100 to the original samples and incubated them at room temperature for 1 ~ 2 min. A subsequent re-analysis was conducted, and the disappearance of the positive signal coupled with an increase in the background signal was indicative of exosomes bearing membranous structures, as opposed to mere protein aggregates.
Co-Immunoprecipitation and Pull-down
The h-AT2 cells were first transfected with MSC-EGFP-Wnt5a-flag plasmids and then extracted proteins after 72 h using NP40 lysis buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology, CHN) supplemented with 1× phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF, Milipore, USA), phostop (Roche, CHE) and phosphatase inhibitor (Roche, CHE). At the meanwhile, flag-beads (Sigma, USA) and IgG-beads (Beyotime Biotechnology, CHN) were washed with NP40 mixture. Proteins were divided into three groups, including Input, IgG and IP. IgG and IP groups were added corresponding beads and incubated overnight in 4 °C. Then, beads were kept after three wash times.
Mix equal volumes and concentrations of recombinant human Wnt5a-GST protein (MCE, USA) and recombinant human ROCK1-His protein (proteintech, CHN), and divide them into three groups: GST-Wnt5a + ROCK1-His (Input) group, IgG group, and GST pull-down group. Add IgG beads and GST beads (MCE, USA) to the IgG and GST pull-down groups, respectively, and incubate at 4 °C overnight. Retain the beads, and after washing three times, store them for later use.
Western Bloting
In each tissue block (0.3 cm × 0.3 cm), 500 µL of lysis buffer (Solarbio, CHN) supplemented with 1× phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF, Milipore, USA), phostop (Roche, CHE) and phosphatase inhibitor (Roche, CHE). The resulting mixture was homogenized, and the lysates were subsequently collected. Any precipitate was removed by centrifugation. Next, 30 µg of the extracted protein was separated on sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gels with a concentration gradient of 10–12%. These proteins were then electrAophoretically transferred onto 0.45 μm PVDF membranes (Millipore, US) and blocked for 1 h in PBS containing 0.5‰ Triton-100 (Solarbio, CHN) and 5% nonfat dry milk. Overnight at 4 °C, the membranes were incubated with primary antibodies, which included monoclonal antibodies against SPC (Sigma, USA), ROCK1 (Cell Signaling Technology, USA) and p-ROCK1 (Invitrogen, USA), polyclonal antibodies against RhoA (Cell Signaling Technology, USA), Wnt5a (abcam, UK), LC3B (Cell Signaling Technology, USA), Atg5 (Abcam, UK), SPB (Santa cruz biotechnology, USA) and ABCA3 (Bioss, CHN), as well as a monoclonal antibody against β-actin (Millipore, US). After incubation with the primary antibodies, the membranes were treated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies (Proteintech Group, USA). Ultimately, protein expression was visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (G: BOX Chemi XRQ, UK).
Animal Model
The experimental mice used in this study were SPF grade C57BL/6J mice, 8–12 weeks old female mice and 10–12 weeks old male mice, weighing 18–22 g, purchased from Jiangsu Zhidiaokang Biotechnology Co., LTD. This animal experiment was approved by the Experimental Animal Ethics Committee of West China Second Hospital of Sichuan University, and all operations were conducted in accordance with relevant animal management regulations. All experimental animals were raised in SPF Laboratory Animal Center, West China Second Hospital, Sichuan University. The mice were more active at night and rested during the day, so they chose to close the cage at 18–19 PM. At 8–9 am the next day, they used a 200 µl gun tip to check the vaginal plugs. If white embolism was seen in the vaginal opening or the 200 µl gun tip was obviously blocked, they were considered pregnant and marked as E0.5 day.
E0.5 day old female and male mice were divided into control group, premature exosome group and full-term exosome group (
n
= 3). The preterm exosome group and term exosome group were injected 100 µL hucMSCs in the tail vein of E10.5 and E15.5, respectively. The exact current exosome concentration was measured by NTA before injection, and the injection was carried out according to the concentration of 2 × 1010/particles/kg. The control group was injected with equal volume DPBS for 2 consecutive days, and the lungs were taken from E13.5 and E18.5 cesarean section.
Lung Tissue Perfusion, Dissection and Histology
After administering 60 mg/kg of pentobarbital intraperitoneally (I.P.) for anesthesia, the lungs were flushed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) via the right ventricle (RV) at a consistent pressure of 20 ~ 25 cmH
2
O. The left lung was meticulously excised and preserved at −80 °C. The right lung was then insufflated in situ with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) to a steady pressure of 15 ~ 20 cmH
2
O before being left to soak overnight in 4% PFA. Following fixation, the lung tissue was transferred to 75% ethanol (EtOH) and processed through a tissue dehydrator (Leica-ASP 6025, GER) for dehydration overnight. The tissue was subsequently embedded in paraffin and sectioned into four separate lobes of the right lung. Finally, the lung tissue was embedded in paraffin for the creation of histological sections.
Lung Parenchymal Morphometry and Immunofluorescence
The lung sections were stained with Hematoxylin & Eosin (H&E) to observe general tissue morphology. Areas from 5 μm thick lung sections were randomly selected and imaged at 200× and 400× magnifications using an Olympus BX53 microscope (Olympus, Japan). Image calibration was conducted with standard micrometer images captured at the same magnification. Immunofluorescence (IF) was employed to investigate the expression and localization of specific markers. Briefly, fresh lung tissue sections were de-paraffinized with xylene and rehydrated. Antigen retrieval was performed in a high-temperature environment using 1×EDTA (Solarbio, CHN), followed by blocking with 5% donkey serum. The sections were then incubated with primary antibodies α-SMA (Abcam, UK), SPC (Sigma, USA), ABCA3 (Bioss, CHN) and Ki67 (Abcam, UK) overnight at 4 ℃. Post-incubation, the sections were washed with 3% PBST and co-incubated with donkey anti-rabbit or mouse secondary antibodies conjugated with different fluorescent dyes and DAPI for 1 h in the dark at room temperature. After washing with 3% PBST, the slides were examined and documented using an FV3000 confocal microscope (Olympus, Japan) a Digital slice scanner (Pannoramic MIDI, HU).
Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were conducted utilizing GraphPad Prism 8.0.2 software (GraphPad Software, USA). The data are represented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) derived from triplicate measurements of independent experiments. To evaluate the differences among groups, two-tailed Student’s t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and two-way ANOVA were employed. Pearson Correlation Coefficient analysis was carried out to investigate the associations between genes. A
p
-value of less than 0.05 was deemed statistically significant.

body:
Introduction
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), is one of the most common diseases of preterm babies, especially in surviving extremely preterm infants who below 28 gestational weeks. The term BPD was first described by Northway et al. [
1
]. in 1967, initially referring to a severe form of chronic lung disease that developed in premature infants with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) requiring prolonged oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation. Despite significant progress in recent years in understanding the pathogenesis, pathology, physiology, clinical characteristics, prevention, and treatment of BPD, the prognosis of BPD remains unfavorable [
2
,
3
]. According to foreign data, the mortality rate of severe BPD is 25%, with 10% occurring in the first year [
2
]. The main causes of death include recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, sepsis, persistent pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary heart disease, and sudden death [
4
]. Different from the old BPD, new type of BPD has been changed to the simplification of alveolar structure, reduction in the number of alveoli, abnormal development of capillaries, and impaired development of lung parenchyma [
5
]. Traditional treatment, therefore, can no longer meet the clinical treatment needs of new BPD, which instead, should focus on promoting the lung development and repair during extrauterine growth. Pulmonary populations in the human lung are diverse and complex, and there are ongoing efforts to develop a complete lung cell atlas [
6
–
8
]. Given this diversity, however, alveolar type II epithelial (AT2) cells are the certain subtypes of pneumonocytes that are vulnerable to damage repair and play a leading role in BPD.
In the last decade, stem cell therapy has made significant progress in promoting tissue development and injury repair. The mechanism of stem cell therapy mainly relies on the paracrine pathway to release extracellular vesicles containing growth factors and cytokines, exerting anti-apoptotic, immune-suppressing, and angiogenic effects, which are increasingly used as an alternative to stem cells for treatment. EVs, also known as exosomes (Exos), with a lipid bilayer membrane containing transmembrane proteins, they can enrich the water-soluble hydrophilic components in the cytoplasm of donor cells [
9
]. It has been proven that human mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (hMSCs-Exos) play a crucial part in promoting alveolar maturation and lung vascular development, alleviating the formation of pulmonary hypertension, regulating the phenotype of lung macrophages, and reducing the formation of lung tissue fibrosis [
10
–
12
]. Nevertheless, the mechanism of exosomes therapy is not well studied.
In this study, starting from the essential issue of BPD in preterm babies, we focused on the extrauterine development of premature alveoli. We found that Exos derived from term infant umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (tiUCMSCs) could obviously promoting fetus lung development, while tiUCMSCs-derived Exos (term-Exos) or preterm infant umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (piUCMSCs)-derived Exos (preterm-Exos) were almost the same in shape, concentration or expression of protein markers. Proteomic sequencing of Exos between these two groups indicated the expression of Wnt5a were different, higher in term-Exos. As we known, the Wnt pathway plays a key role in maintaining cell stemness and determining cell fate, including both classical (Wnt/β-catenin dependent) and non-classical (β-catenin independent) pathways [
13
]. As a representative of activating non-classical pathways among the Wnt protein family, Wnt5a can directly regulate the fate of stem cell differentiation through Wnt5a/PCP and Wnt5a/Ca
2+
, and also interact with the classical Wnt pathway represented by Wnt3a to indirectly regulate stem cell differentiation [
13
–
15
]. Through coIP and pull-down techniques, we found a direct interaction between Wnt5a and Rho-associated protein kinase 1 (ROCK1), which probably via promoting phosphorylation of ROCK1. Next, back to mice we detected the expression change of RhoA, SPC and SPB, microtubule-associated proteins 1 A/1B light chain 3B (LC3B), ATP-binding cassette transporter A3 (ABCA3) in lung tissue, almost presenting higher expressions in term-Exos groups.
To sum up, these results had showed the efficacy of exosomes in the treatment of BPD and revealed the underlying mechanism in the aspect between exosomal Wnt5a and lung development, providing a theoretical foundation for our further research.
Results
No Significant Differences were Found in Phenotypes Between term-Exos and preterm-Exos
Studies have shown that there are differences in the number, expression, and function of genes between full-term infants and preterm infants [
16
], and the exosomes derived from them may also be different accordingly. Therefore, for a better research about the function of hucMSCs-Exos, we first successfully extracted and cultured the hucMSCs from healthy term and preterm infants’ umbilical cords on birth. Afterwards, hucMSCs were characterized by examining the differentiation identification of osteogenesis, lipogenesis and chondrogenesis, as well as detecting their positive and negative markers via flow cytometry, which showed markers CD105, CD73, CD44, CD90 were positive and markers CD11b, CD31 were negative (Figure
S1
).
After that, exosomes were extracted through ultra-centrifugation from both the tiUCMSCs and piUCMCSs (Figure
S2
A). NTA and TEM of fresh exosomes in two groups both revealed a heterogeneous exosomes population occupied the average diameter of 150 nm and proved to the typical morphological features of exosomes, which were almost no differences in these two groups (Fig.
1
A, B). To further verify that exosomes were membrane structure but not the protein aggregates, we examined the typical markers CD9, CD63 and CD81 of exosomes via nanoflow technique (Fig.
1
C). For more rigorous follow-up experiments, we compared the particles and diameters of exosomes conserved in three different temperatures, 4 ℃, −80 ℃ and liquid nitrogen for 7 days respectively. We found that there were no significant differences in diameters among these three temperatures for short period, however, the particles in 4 ℃ group performed the most (Fig.
1
D, E), providing the evidence to support the stability of exosomes for our subsequent experiments. Through western blotting method, Exos associated markers CD9, CD63 and TSG101 were expressed while being negative for calnexin (Fig.
1
F), and there were little differences between two groups either. To demonstrate that both groups of exosomes can be taken up by cell, we used two membrane dyes simultaneously. Successfully demonstrated exosomes not membrane dyes themselves could be taken by cells, we observed there were no obvious differences between two groups’ exosomes in cellular uptake (Fig.
1
G, H). Furthermore, with the assistance of phalloidin, we captured that not only could exosomes be taken up by cells, but also, they could break through the nuclear membrane (Fig.
1
I).

Term-Exos Obviously Accelerated the Fetus Lung Development
To verify whether Exos in two distinct groups have different roles in lung development, we first observed that in A549 cells via CCK-8 method, and found both groups exosomes could promote the proliferation, of which in term-Exos group was more efficient (Fig.
2
A). Then, we injected exosomes of two groups respectively via tail vein when mice were pregnant in day 10.5 and 15.5, and harvested the fetal lung tissue 48 h after 2 doses (Fig.
2
B). It is well known that the expression level of α-SMA increases with the maturation of lung tissue during lung development [
17
,
18
]. In our model, we found an obvious overexpression of α-SMA and a higher degree of alveolation in E18.5 lung tissue with 2 doses of term-Exos (Fig.
2
C, D), inferring a potential effect of term-Exos in fetus lung development. Subsequently, the ultrastructure of alveolar epithelial cells was examined under transmission electron microscope (TME). Compared with the control, the glycogen of AT2 cells in fetal lung tissue of the term-Exos group was significantly reduced, while the number of lamellar bodies (LBs) increased and the structure was more complete (Fig.
2
E), further confirmed the role of promoting lung development. Moreover, the expressions of ABCA3, Ki67 and SPC were obviously accelerated in term-Exos group (Fig.
2
F), indicating the higher alveolarization level.

Term-Exos Promoted the Expression of Lung Development Related Proteins
As the most important marker of AT2 cells, the level of SPC expression has been highly correlated with the degree of alveolar development. To further identify term-Exos could promote the lung development, we examined the expression of SPC. We found the protein expression was both increased in term-Exos group at E13.5 and E18.5, while gene expression was firstly suppressed at E13.5 but accelerated at E18.5 (Fig.
3
A, B and D). RhoA and its family, responsible in the regulation of pulmonary endothelial and smooth muscle cell [
19
], are intimately related to the lung development. In our results, term-Exos could promoted the RhoA expression in early stage of fetus, while preterm-Exos decreased the mRNA expression of RhoA (Fig.
3
A, B and E). Meanwhile, as the markers of AT2 cells development, expression of ABCA3 and mature SPB were both increased in term-Exos group (Fig.
3
C, F).

Discussion
In this study, we used the fetal mice to assess the competence of UCMSCs-Exos to participate in lung development. As mentioned earlier, due to the limitations of the preterm infant’s developmental stage and repair capacity, children with BPD are at risk of respiratory issues later on, stemming from immature lung development and the inability of lung tissue to repair promptly after injury. It is essential to fully harness and guide their repair potential to promote the formation of new alveoli and the repair of damaged lung tissue, meanwhile minimizing drug-induced side effects and complications. Here, we focused our analysis on the possible mechanisms by which UCMSCs-Exos are mined in promoting lung development. Although the phenotypes of Exos in two groups were no significant differences, term-Exos could obviously promote the process of alveolarization in fetal mice. We further demonstrated that Wnt5a naturally rich in term-Exos were probably responsible for that. Wnt5a could directly interact with the ROCK1 and promote its phosphorylation as well as the development of LBs to accelerate the fetus lung development.
The Wnt signaling pathway is crucial for various developmental processes, including lung development. It can be broadly classified into two categories: canonical Wnt signaling and non-canonical Wnt signaling. Canonical Wnt signaling is primarily mediated through the β-catenin pathway. When Wnt ligands (such as Wnt3a) bind to their Frizzled receptors, this leads to the stabilization of β-catenin in the cytoplasm [
25
]. The stabilized β-catenin translocate to the nucleus, where it interacts with TCF/LEF transcription factors to activate the expression of target genes. Compared to canonical Wnt signaling pathway, non-canonical Wnt signaling is often thought of as the β-catenin independent pathway. In the non-canonical pathway of Wnt, Wnt5a/PCP is initiated by the binding of Wnt ligands to Frizzled receptors (Fig.
7
), which can alter the myosin cytoskeleton to coordinate the directed motility of cells [
5
]. Both pathways can co-regulate specific genes involved in lung development. For example, the activities of these pathways can influence the expression of growth factors and transcription factors necessary for lung epithelial and mesenchymal cell identity [
26
]. The activation of one pathway can influence the other. For instance, non-canonical Wnt signaling might modulate the effects of β-catenin on target gene expression or vice versa, creating a feedback loop that helps fine-tune lung development [
27
]. Wnt signaling pathways interact with other signaling pathways (like FGF, BMP, or Shh) during lung development, adding an extra layer of regulation that involves both canonical and non-canonical inputs [
28
]. In our results, we first found the top 15 expressions in differential proteins, and then we found the epithelial cells development pathway via GO enrichment (Figure
S4
). Next, we found Wnt5a in this pathway. Further PPI analysis indicated naturally Wnt5a in term-Exos could obviously promote the fetus lung development probably related to its regulatory network (Figure
S4
). In these data, for instance, the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) has been demonstrated to play an important role in in lung development and regeneration of tracheal epithelium from basal stem cells [
29
], displaying the powerful control network of Wnt5a.
Fig. 7
A schematic model showing the proposed mechanism for the role of exosomal Wnt5a in lung development. Term-Exos: Term infant umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells-derived exosomes, Ror: Receptor tyrosine kinase-like orphan receptor; FZD

Wnt5a activates this pathway through interaction with Frizzled receptors and co-receptors like ROR2, leading to the activation of small GTPases, such as Rho and Rac, which orchestrate cytoskeletal rearrangements [
30
]. Additionally, Wnt5a can influence intracellular calcium levels, promoting calcium-dependent signaling that affects various cellular functions, including gene expression and cell migration [
31
]. It is a fundamental, conserved, yet essential regulatory pathway that plays a crucial role in regulating lung development. Guo et al. [
32
]. discovered through single-cell RNA-Seq analysis of neonatal lung tissue after birth that a small number of alveolar epithelial cells contain
Wnt5a
transcript sequences, suggesting that Wnt5a is involved in the alveolar development process. Ghosh et al. have reported that Wnt5a-induced non-canonical Wnt signaling may play an important role in the process of AT2 to AT1 cell transdifferentiation [
33
], indicating Wnt5a could further activate the self-repair ability of alveolar epithelial cells and ultimately promote the repair of alveolar damage. During embryonic development, Wnt5a exhibits dynamic expression patterns that are crucial for the proper morphogenesis of the pulmonary system. Studies have demonstrated that Wnt5a expression is temporally regulated, with significant upregulation during key stages of lung development, particularly during the pseudoglandular and canalicular stages. This expression is essential for alveolar epithelial cell differentiation and the overall architecture of the lung. For instance, Wnt5a is involved in the regulation of mesenchymal-epithelial interactions, which are vital for alveologenesis, the process of alveolar formation. Disruption of Wnt5a signaling can lead to severe developmental defects, highlighting its indispensable role in lung embryogenesis [
34
]. Our results described that compared with preterm-Exos group, term-Exos groups have higher concentration of Wnt5a, following a higher level of alveolarization and more intact LBs in AT2 cells of fetal mice. Furthermore, in the context of fetal mice lung tissue, Wnt5a has been shown to promote the expression of several key markers, such as Ki67, SPC, and ABCA3, suggesting that Wnt5a are capable of accelerating the lung maturity. It is well known Ki67 is a well-known marker of cell proliferation. In fetal lung tissue, Wnt5a can stimulate progenitor cells to divide and differentiate, thereby enhancing the overall cell population necessary for proper lung development. Increased Ki67 expression indicates a higher proliferation rate in the lung epithelium, which is crucial for the formation of the complex structures of the alveoli. SPC is a key marker of AT2 cells, which are responsible for producing surfactant-a substance critical for reducing surface tension in the lungs, thereby preventing alveolar collapse and facilitating proper gas exchange after birth. Wnt5a can promote the differentiation of progenitor cells into type II alveolar cells, thus increasing the expression of SPC. This process is essential for preparing the lungs for functional maturity just before birth. Studies have demonstrated that Wnt5a expression is temporally regulated, with significant upregulation during key stages of lung development, particularly during the pseudoglandular and canalicular stages. This expression is essential for alveolar epithelial cell differentiation and the overall architecture of the lung. ABCA3 is an important protein involved in surfactant metabolism and lipid trafficking in AT2 cells. Its expression is crucial for the synthesis and secretion of surfactant lipids, which are essential for lung function. Wnt5a may enhance the development of AT2 cells and promote the ABCA3 expression, thereby supporting the proper assembly and secretion of surfactant in the developing lung tissue. This is vital for lung function and overall respiratory health.
In our study, we also found an increase of expression of RhoA mainly in E13.5 fetal lung tissue after term-Exos treatment, as well as the increased expressions of SPC, SPB and ABCA3. As a member of the Rho family of small GTPases, RhoA is a central regulatory factor in regulating vascular permeability through cytoskeletal rearrangement [
35
]. It can also promote alveolar epithelial cell homeostasis via Mer/RhoA [
36
], thereby facilitating alveolar growth and playing a significant role in lung development and repair processes. Nevertheless, there was not obvious direct interaction between Wnt5a and RhoA, verified by CoIP experiment (Figure
S2
E). ROCK family is well known as the Rho-kinase, a serine/threonine kinase from the AGC (cAMP-dependent protein kinase A/protein kinase G/protein kinase C) kinase family, mainly including ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms [
37
,
38
]. ROCK1 has been previously considered to be activated when bound to the GTP-bound form of RhoA. Interestingly, we found Wnt5a could directly interact with ROCK1 via promoting its phosphorylation in human AT2 cells, indicating Wnt5a could activate ROCK1 with an RhoA-independent way. An early study has demonstrated that ROCK1 could mediate upstream Rac1 and RhoA activity and then regulate actin cytoskeleton reorganization processes [
39
], which was consistent with our results showing an increase expression of α-SMA in lung tissue of term-Exos group. α-SMA, also known as ACTA2, is one of the marker proteins of myofibroblasts. Myofibroblasts play a crucial role in lung development, participating in the formation and maturation of alveoli as well as the maintenance of lung tissue structure [
40
]. Therefore, it is rational to suppose that term-Exos could improve the expression of RhoA to accelerate lung development regulated by Wnt5a/ROCK1 pathway.
As the hallmark of AT2 cells, LBs are the main place for the storage and secretion of alveolar surfactant phospholipids. It is a consensus that surfactant plays a vital part in reducing surface tension at the air-liquid interface of the alveolar wall, thus preventing alveolar collapse and transudation of capillary fluid into the alveolar lumen [
41
]. Located on the limiting membrane of the LB, phosphatidylcholine transfer to LBs requires an adenosine triphosphate ABCA3
42
. Surfactant proteins proSPB and proSPC trafficking from the ER are proteolytically processed during transport to LBs, then he active peptides, mature surfactant proteins (SPB and SPC), are assembled with surfactant phospholipids into membranes that are stored in LBs [
42
]. In clinical treatment of preterm babies, early adequate supplementation of alveolar surfactant phospholipids has been demonstrated to be an effective way to prevent RDS and subsequent BPD [
43
,
44
]. As we described before, LBs were considered a special type of autophagosome [
23
,
24
]. Proteins ABCA3 and SPB are believed to play important roles in the development of LBs and the formation of pulmonary surfactant [
45
]. Li et al. [
24
] found that in
Atg7
knockout mice, there was abnormal lung morphological development, the autophagic process was impaired, and there was a decrease in the expression of SPB, as well as a reduction in the number and volume of lamellar bodies. Similarly, our results also revealed that the expression of LC3B was increased in term-Exos group, indicating AT2 cells autophagy was including in the process of the LBs development. Interestingly, in this study, we also found the expression of Atg5 in fetal development early stage was increased by preterm-Exos, which decreased Atg5 expression reversely. Early research revealed that the Atg12 system is located upstream of the LC3B system in the context of ATG protein organization, Atg12 is finally conjugated to Atg5, forming the irreversible ATG12-ATG5 complex, which strongly enhances the formation of LC3B-phosphatidylethanolamine conjugation [
46
]. Therefore, we supposed that Wnt5a could regulate the LC3B dependent autophagy via an Atg5 complex pathway. In our study, not only the expressions of LBs related proteins such as SPC, SPB and ABCA3 have been increased by term-Exos, but also term-Exos promoted the development of LBs, helping premature alveoli secrete more surfactant to maintain the alveolar surface tension.
In a nutshell, it is reasonable to conclude that term-Exos could promote alveolar development via self-enriched Wnt5a at least two functions. First, term-Exos could improve the expression of RhoA to accelerate lung development regulated by Wnt5a/ROCK1 pathway. Secondly, term-Exos could promote the development of LBs and the expression of LBs related proteins to maintain the alveolar surface tension and accelerate the lung maturation.
Materials and Methods
Study and Approval
Human umbilical cord was acquired from term and preterm infants on birth (all individuals and their parents provided informed consent to participate in this study and approval was provided by Medical Research Ethics Committee of West China Second University Hospital, Sichuan University, Medical Research 2022 Ethics Approval No. 290). All animal experiments have been approved by the China Ethics Committee and West China Second University Hospital Institutional Animal Care, and performed in accordance with the ethical standards, and raised in Animal Care.
Primary Cell Culture
The hucMSCs were isolated and cultured following a modified explant method, as described in our last study. In summary, the umbilical cord was cleaned with Dulbecco’s phosphate-buffered saline (DPBS, Invitrogen, USA), then longitudinally cut, and the arteries and veins were all removed. Following that, the soft gel tissues were dissected into small pieces (1 ~ 3 mm [
3
]) and placed individually on 6-well plate with Modified Eagle Medium-α (MEM-α, Gibco, USA), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Invitrogen, USA) and penicillin/streptomycin. The plates were then incubated for 10 ~ 12 days at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO
2
. During the incubation period, supplemented MEM-α was periodically added, until the umbilical cord tissue was eventually removed. After washing the plates three times with MEM-α, the plastic adherent cell colonies were trypsinized (TrypLE™ Express (1X), Gibco, USA) and maintained in culture using MEM-α supplemented with 10% FBS and penicillin/streptomycin. At passage 3 ~ 5, hucMSCs were expanded in 10-stack Corning CellSTACK
®
cell culture chambers. It is important to note that multiple umbilical cords were used, with each cord giving rise to individual MSC colonies. Each independent in vivo experiment utilized a distinct Exos preparation.
Exos Harvest and Isolation
The isolation and characterization of Exos were carried out in accordance with the guidelines provided by the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles (ISEV) in their 2018 Minimal Information for Studies of Extracellular Vesicles (MISEV) publications [
47
,
48
]. Exos, denoting small EVs (sEVs) with diameters ranging approximately between 40 and 150 nm, along with the expression of well-characterized Exos markers such as TSG101, ALIX, CD9, CD63, CD81, and Flotillin-1 (FLOT-1), were procured from the conditioned media (CM) of hucMSCs cultures. These cultures were maintained for 48 h in serum-free media. The isolation process involved sequential differential centrifugation procedures to sequentially eliminate cells (750 ×g for 10 min), cellular debris (3000 ×g for 20 min), and apoptotic remnants (12,000 ×g for 45 min), all of which were conducted under strictly controlled 4℃ conditions. Subsequently, the CM underwent ultra-centrifugation using a Type50.2 Ti rotor for a duration of 1.5 h at 120,000 ×g and 4 °C. The resulting pellet was meticulously collected and then transferred to a SW41 Ti rotor for an additional centrifugation period of 2 h at the same speed and temperature. Finally, the supernatants were carefully removed, and the Exos pellet was re-suspended in 200 µL of Dulbecco’s Phosphate-Buffered Saline (DPBS, Invitrogen, USA).
Transmission Electron Microscopy
To evaluate the morphology of Exos, a 5 µL sample from the sEV preparation was adsorbed onto a carbon-coated grid (Electron Microscopy Sciences, USA) for a duration of one minute. The grids were rendered hydrophilic through a 30-seconds exposure to glow discharge. Any surplus liquid was then carefully eliminated, and the grids were subsequently cleansed with a single drop of water. Following the removal of any remaining excess liquid, the grids were stained with 1% uranyl acetate for a period of 15 s. The morphology of the adsorbed Exos was subsequently examined under a transmission electron microscopy (JEM-1400FLASH, JP).
For lung tissue observation, the following steps are used to conduct the experiment: Fixation: The samples were pre-fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde (customer’s fixation), followed by postfixation with 1% osmium tetroxide. Dehydration: The samples were dehydrated stepwise with acetone, with the dehydration agent concentration gradient of 30% → 50% → 70% → 80% → 90% → 95% → 100% (change the 100% concentration three times). Infiltration: The dehydration agent and Epon-812 embedding medium were mixed in proportions of 3:1, 1:1, and 1:3, respectively, for sequential infiltration. Embedding: The sample was embedded with pure Epon-812 embedding medium. Semi-thin localization and ultra-thin sectioning: the mouse lung tissue alveolar region was selected under a light microscope by observing semi-thin sections, and ultra-thin sections of 60 ~ 90 nm were cut using an ultra-thin sectioning machine and collected on copper grids. Staining: The sections were first stained with uranyl acetate for 10 ~ 15 min, followed by staining with lead citrate for 1 ~ 2 min at room temperature. Next, using the JEM-1400FLASH transmission electron microscope (TOK, JP) to collect images of the copper mesh, each copper mesh is first observed in low magnification to view the entire tissue, then images of the areas to be observed are collected, and specific lesions are examined.
Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis
The size and concentration distributions of Exos were meticulously assessed using NTA (ZetaView, Particle Metrix, GER) on a state-of-the-art Nanoparticle Tracking Analyses system, adhering to the method previously outlined [
49
]. During the procedure, the samples were introduced into the pump, and the Brownian motion of the nanoparticles was meticulously monitored. Concurrently, the particle size was determined based on the Stokes-Einstein equation, while the particle concentration in the solution was accurately computed from the number of tracked particles. Prior to analysis, the Exos samples were carefully diluted in vesicle-free ultrapure water to ensure optimal measurement conditions.
Exosomes Markers Characterization
We commenced the characterization of the isolated exosomes by employing conventional methodologies, initiating with WB analysis on the extracted exosomes. We utilized CD9, CD63, and TSG101 (Abiowell, CHN) as our positive markers, with Calnexin (Abiowell, CHN) serving as the negative control. To discern exosomes from protein aggregates, we resorted to nanoparticle flow cytometry for the analysis of the exosomes’ surface markers. Post-determination of concentration via NTA, the samples were adjusted to a concentration of 1 × 10
7
particles/mL using DPBS. A 100 µL aliquot of this diluted sample was then incubated at ambient temperature, shielded from light, with 5 µL each of PE-conjugated CD9, PE-conjugated CD63, and APC-conjugated CD81 antibodies (Invitrogen, USA) for a duration of 45 min. To ensure adequate mixing, the samples were subjected to intermittent shaking throughout the incubation period. For flow cytometric analysis, we utilized the Cytoflex instrument (Beckman Coulter, USA), equipped with a 405/10 filter and the Event Rate set to a high level. The detection of scatter signals was optimized using the VSSC-H parameter, with the threshold configured to Height. Prior to analysis, the instrument was meticulously cleaned with a 1% sodium hypochlorite solution, filtered through a 0.1 μm Millex-VV syringe filter unit from Merck, followed by a rinse with ultrapure water, also filtered through a Millex-VV syringe filter. Calibration of the optical path was achieved using particle beads (ApogeeMix, ESP). Upon the detection of positive signals, data were meticulously collected and recorded. Subsequently, we introduced 0.1% Triton X-100 to the original samples and incubated them at room temperature for 1 ~ 2 min. A subsequent re-analysis was conducted, and the disappearance of the positive signal coupled with an increase in the background signal was indicative of exosomes bearing membranous structures, as opposed to mere protein aggregates.
Co-Immunoprecipitation and Pull-down
The h-AT2 cells were first transfected with MSC-EGFP-Wnt5a-flag plasmids and then extracted proteins after 72 h using NP40 lysis buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology, CHN) supplemented with 1× phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF, Milipore, USA), phostop (Roche, CHE) and phosphatase inhibitor (Roche, CHE). At the meanwhile, flag-beads (Sigma, USA) and IgG-beads (Beyotime Biotechnology, CHN) were washed with NP40 mixture. Proteins were divided into three groups, including Input, IgG and IP. IgG and IP groups were added corresponding beads and incubated overnight in 4 °C. Then, beads were kept after three wash times.
Mix equal volumes and concentrations of recombinant human Wnt5a-GST protein (MCE, USA) and recombinant human ROCK1-His protein (proteintech, CHN), and divide them into three groups: GST-Wnt5a + ROCK1-His (Input) group, IgG group, and GST pull-down group. Add IgG beads and GST beads (MCE, USA) to the IgG and GST pull-down groups, respectively, and incubate at 4 °C overnight. Retain the beads, and after washing three times, store them for later use.
Western Bloting
In each tissue block (0.3 cm × 0.3 cm), 500 µL of lysis buffer (Solarbio, CHN) supplemented with 1× phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF, Milipore, USA), phostop (Roche, CHE) and phosphatase inhibitor (Roche, CHE). The resulting mixture was homogenized, and the lysates were subsequently collected. Any precipitate was removed by centrifugation. Next, 30 µg of the extracted protein was separated on sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gels with a concentration gradient of 10–12%. These proteins were then electrAophoretically transferred onto 0.45 μm PVDF membranes (Millipore, US) and blocked for 1 h in PBS containing 0.5‰ Triton-100 (Solarbio, CHN) and 5% nonfat dry milk. Overnight at 4 °C, the membranes were incubated with primary antibodies, which included monoclonal antibodies against SPC (Sigma, USA), ROCK1 (Cell Signaling Technology, USA) and p-ROCK1 (Invitrogen, USA), polyclonal antibodies against RhoA (Cell Signaling Technology, USA), Wnt5a (abcam, UK), LC3B (Cell Signaling Technology, USA), Atg5 (Abcam, UK), SPB (Santa cruz biotechnology, USA) and ABCA3 (Bioss, CHN), as well as a monoclonal antibody against β-actin (Millipore, US). After incubation with the primary antibodies, the membranes were treated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies (Proteintech Group, USA). Ultimately, protein expression was visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (G: BOX Chemi XRQ, UK).
Animal Model
The experimental mice used in this study were SPF grade C57BL/6J mice, 8–12 weeks old female mice and 10–12 weeks old male mice, weighing 18–22 g, purchased from Jiangsu Zhidiaokang Biotechnology Co., LTD. This animal experiment was approved by the Experimental Animal Ethics Committee of West China Second Hospital of Sichuan University, and all operations were conducted in accordance with relevant animal management regulations. All experimental animals were raised in SPF Laboratory Animal Center, West China Second Hospital, Sichuan University. The mice were more active at night and rested during the day, so they chose to close the cage at 18–19 PM. At 8–9 am the next day, they used a 200 µl gun tip to check the vaginal plugs. If white embolism was seen in the vaginal opening or the 200 µl gun tip was obviously blocked, they were considered pregnant and marked as E0.5 day.
E0.5 day old female and male mice were divided into control group, premature exosome group and full-term exosome group (
n
= 3). The preterm exosome group and term exosome group were injected 100 µL hucMSCs in the tail vein of E10.5 and E15.5, respectively. The exact current exosome concentration was measured by NTA before injection, and the injection was carried out according to the concentration of 2 × 1010/particles/kg. The control group was injected with equal volume DPBS for 2 consecutive days, and the lungs were taken from E13.5 and E18.5 cesarean section.
Lung Tissue Perfusion, Dissection and Histology
After administering 60 mg/kg of pentobarbital intraperitoneally (I.P.) for anesthesia, the lungs were flushed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) via the right ventricle (RV) at a consistent pressure of 20 ~ 25 cmH
2
O. The left lung was meticulously excised and preserved at −80 °C. The right lung was then insufflated in situ with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) to a steady pressure of 15 ~ 20 cmH
2
O before being left to soak overnight in 4% PFA. Following fixation, the lung tissue was transferred to 75% ethanol (EtOH) and processed through a tissue dehydrator (Leica-ASP 6025, GER) for dehydration overnight. The tissue was subsequently embedded in paraffin and sectioned into four separate lobes of the right lung. Finally, the lung tissue was embedded in paraffin for the creation of histological sections.
Lung Parenchymal Morphometry and Immunofluorescence
The lung sections were stained with Hematoxylin & Eosin (H&E) to observe general tissue morphology. Areas from 5 μm thick lung sections were randomly selected and imaged at 200× and 400× magnifications using an Olympus BX53 microscope (Olympus, Japan). Image calibration was conducted with standard micrometer images captured at the same magnification. Immunofluorescence (IF) was employed to investigate the expression and localization of specific markers. Briefly, fresh lung tissue sections were de-paraffinized with xylene and rehydrated. Antigen retrieval was performed in a high-temperature environment using 1×EDTA (Solarbio, CHN), followed by blocking with 5% donkey serum. The sections were then incubated with primary antibodies α-SMA (Abcam, UK), SPC (Sigma, USA), ABCA3 (Bioss, CHN) and Ki67 (Abcam, UK) overnight at 4 ℃. Post-incubation, the sections were washed with 3% PBST and co-incubated with donkey anti-rabbit or mouse secondary antibodies conjugated with different fluorescent dyes and DAPI for 1 h in the dark at room temperature. After washing with 3% PBST, the slides were examined and documented using an FV3000 confocal microscope (Olympus, Japan) a Digital slice scanner (Pannoramic MIDI, HU).
Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were conducted utilizing GraphPad Prism 8.0.2 software (GraphPad Software, USA). The data are represented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) derived from triplicate measurements of independent experiments. To evaluate the differences among groups, two-tailed Student’s t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and two-way ANOVA were employed. Pearson Correlation Coefficient analysis was carried out to investigate the associations between genes. A
p
-value of less than 0.05 was deemed statistically significant.
